rv.q: In the end, it's a play that takes on rather more than the structure can hold. But it honours both family and found family, cherishes the bravery of ordinary people in the face of adversity and prejudice, celebrates acceptance and is written with huge heart and wit.

In the 1990s, matriarch Eileen (Lindsey Coulson) has just died. Her three daughters and mixed-race grandson Ted (Leo Whitfield Harris, making his stage debut) are left with the routine sadmin of bereavement, and the emotional reckoning that goes with it; the women’s husbands are variously useless.
Ilford Boy is an imperfect, but gorgeous little production.

Wynter himself grew up in east London and presumably pours some of his own experiences into what ultimately unwinds as a by-turns acutely funny and desperately sad tapestry of a very particular time and place.
It doesn’t travel quite as far as it might, but it’s a hugely entertaining journey.
It’s a shame that Ilford Boy doesn’t quite lean into what makes it such a powerful and thought-provoking premise, but even with that, it’s well worth the watch.
Ilford Boy is more focused and successful and marks him out as a new writer to watch out for and be excited for his future work.

cn.t: Danny Lee Wynter's autobiographical drama impresses with vivid writing and heartfelt performances, though its meandering structure keeps it from full cohesion. Critics praise the truthfulness and humor that make its narrative flaws forgivable.
